nutshell: Not person ReID - this is an animal re-identification infrastructure paper. It introduces WildlifeDatasets, a Python toolkit that unifies 31 public animal re-id datasets under one API (download, preprocessing, standardized splits, matching), and uses it to train MegaDescriptor, the first general-purpose foundation model for individual animal re-identification across species, which substantially outperforms zero-shot CLIP and DINOv2.
contributions: WildlifeDatasets toolkit: unified Python access to 31 public wildlife re-id datasets with standardized closed-set, open-set, disjoint-set, and time-aware train/test splitting, plus a high-level matching API - addressing a real fragmentation problem where prior work used inconsistent, poorly curated, per-species dataset setups.

The largest reported empirical comparison in this space: SIFT and Superpoint local descriptors vs. ArcFace and Triplet-loss metric learning (Swin-B vs. EfficientNet-B3 backbones) across 29 datasets, via a 2088-run hyperparameter grid search, establishing ArcFace + Swin-B as the best general-purpose recipe.

MegaDescriptor: the first foundation model for individual re-identification spanning many animal species (Swin-Small/Medium/Large, ArcFace-trained jointly on all 29 datasets), released publicly on HuggingFace, outperforming ImageNet-, CLIP-, and DINOv2-based zero-shot descriptors on every one of the 29 evaluated datasets.

A seen/unseen-domain generalization experiment (cattle datasets held out) showing MegaDescriptor retains meaningfully better performance than DINOv2/CLIP even on species/domains excluded from its training data.
deficiencies: The headline comparison in Table 4 pits MegaDescriptor - explicitly trained/fine-tuned on all 29 evaluation datasets - against CLIP, DINOv2, and ImageNet used purely zero-shot with no wildlife-specific fine-tuning. Calling this an outperformance 'by a significant margin' over those pretrained models is not an apples-to-apples comparison; it mainly shows that in-domain fine-tuning beats out-of-domain zero-shot transfer, which is expected.

The hyperparameter grid search (Fig. 6) shows the best ArcFace configuration has a 25th/75th percentile accuracy of only 49.2%/96.4% (median 87.3%) across the 29 datasets, and three configurations catastrophically diverged to 4-6.4% mean accuracy - this huge dataset-to-dataset variance is shown but never diagnosed (which datasets/species drive it, why).

The paper's own Table 3 acknowledges the Giraffes dataset's ground-truth labels were themselves generated using local descriptors, which inflates local-descriptor accuracy on that dataset - yet this known contamination isn't excluded when concluding 'metric learning approaches outperformed local-feature methods on most datasets.'

Even with the best model (MegaDescriptor-L), several datasets remain quite weak (BelugaID 66.5%, NOAARightWhale 40.3%, LionData 25.2%, HappyWhale 34.3%, NyalaData 36.5%) - the 'consistent state-of-the-art performance on all datasets' framing in the abstract undersells this wide remaining spread.
notable: Useful benchmark-hygiene contribution buried in the results: the paper explicitly identifies several datasets (AerialCattle2017, SMALST, MacaqueFaces, Giraffes, AAUZebraFish) as already solved or near-ceiling and recommends dropping them from future method development/benchmarking - a concrete, actionable recommendation rarely offered this directly in benchmark papers. Also notable: despite metric learning being clearly superior in this paper's own experiments, the tools ecologists actually use in practice (WildID, HotSpotter, I3S) are all still local-feature-based - a real adoption gap between CV research and applied ecology tooling that the paper points out but doesn't attempt to close.

results.setting: MegaDescriptor-L (Swin-L/p4-w12-384), jointly trained/evaluated on all 29 datasets
